variants.title: Trace the request
variants.context: A request is one attempt by a client to use a service. The service interprets it and reads durable data when it needs to.
variants.prompt: A user opens a short link and there is no cache. Build the path up to the moment the service can answer.

items.text: The service receives the request and interprets it.
The browser sends a request for the short link.
The service asks the database for the saved destination.
The database returns the saved destination.

variants.hint: Nothing can be looked up before the request has arrived and been understood.
variants.explanation: The client asks, the service interprets, and only then does it read the durable record it needs.

variants.title: Trace the request
variants.context: A request is one attempt by a client to use a service. The service interprets it and reads durable data when it needs to.
variants.prompt: A user opens a product page. Build only the part of the path that happens before the database has answered.

items.text: The service receives the request and checks it is valid.
The service asks the database for the product record.
The browser sends a request for the product page.

variants.hint: Stop at the moment the question reaches the database.
variants.explanation: Validation belongs to the service, before it spends a database read on a request it should have rejected.

variants.title: Trace the request
variants.context: A request is one attempt by a client to use a service. The service interprets it and reads durable data when it needs to.
variants.prompt: Someone creates a new short link instead of opening one. Build the write path.

items.text: The service writes the record to the database.
The service checks that the request is valid.
The database confirms that the write is stored.
The browser sends the new link to the service.

variants.hint: The service should not promise the link exists before the record is stored.
variants.explanation: Confirm to the user only after the durable write succeeds, or you may promise something that was never saved.

variants.title: Trace the response
variants.context: A response carries the result back to the requester. Work the user is not waiting for can happen after the response is sent.
variants.prompt: The database has found the saved destination. Put the rest of the journey in order.

items.text: The browser follows the redirect to the saved destination.
The database returns the record to the service.
The service sends a redirect response to the browser.

variants.hint: The browser can only act on something it has received.
variants.explanation: The service turns the stored record into the response the client expects.

variants.title: Trace the response
variants.context: A response carries the result back to the requester. Work the user is not waiting for can happen after the response is sent.
variants.prompt: This time a cached copy answered the read and the database was never contacted. Put the response in order.

items.text: The service sends a redirect response to the browser.
The cache returns the copy to the service.
The browser follows the redirect to the saved destination.

variants.hint: Ask which component supplied the value on this path.
variants.explanation: The client cannot tell where the value came from, because the response contract is the same on a hit and a miss.

variants.title: Trace the response
variants.context: A response carries the result back to the requester. Work the user is not waiting for can happen after the response is sent.
variants.prompt: The product also counts every click, but the user must not wait for it. Put the work in order.

items.text: The browser follows the redirect to the destination.
The click is queued for a job that records it later.
The service sends the redirect response to the browser.

variants.hint: Only one of these is something the user is waiting for.
variants.explanation: Counting the click is valuable but not part of a correct redirect, so it happens after the response.

variants.title: Survive a restart
variants.context: Durable storage keeps data when a process stops; memory does not. A second running copy is not a backup, and a timeout does not prove a write failed.
variants.prompt: Your service keeps each new short link in a local variable, and a restart loses them all. What should change?
options: Keep a second copy in another variable in the same process.
Ask the browser to send the link again after each restart.
Write the record to durable storage before confirming success.
optionFeedback: A second variable dies with the process that holds it.
The browser cannot restore data it was told was saved.
The record then outlives the process that created it.
variants.hint: Which option puts the record outside the process that can restart?
variants.explanation: Confirm success only once the record is somewhere that survives the process.

variants.title: Survive a restart
variants.context: Durable storage keeps data when a process stops; memory does not. A second running copy is not a backup, and a timeout does not prove a write failed.
variants.prompt: A teammate says the second running copy of the database makes backups unnecessary. Are they right?
options: No, because a replica copies deletions and corruption too.
Yes, because two live copies mean the data cannot be lost.
Yes, provided the two copies sit in different buildings.
optionFeedback: Backups and a rehearsed restore cover what replication cannot.
A mistaken deletion is applied to every replica at once.
Distance protects against outages, not against a bad write.
variants.hint: What happens on the second copy when a record is deleted by mistake?
variants.explanation: Replicas protect availability; backups and a tested restore protect the data itself.

variants.title: Survive a restart
variants.context: Durable storage keeps data when a process stops; memory does not. A second running copy is not a backup, and a timeout does not prove a write failed.
variants.prompt: A write times out, the service immediately repeats it, and a duplicate link appears. What went wrong?
options: A timeout does not prove the write failed, so retries need a key.
The database was simply too slow and needs replacing with a faster one.
A write that fails once should never be retried by the service at all.
optionFeedback: The first write may have landed after the client stopped waiting.
Speed is not what turned one link into two.
Retrying is safe when the repeated work cannot apply twice.
variants.hint: What do you actually know when a call times out?
variants.explanation: A timeout says you stopped waiting, not that the work did not happen.
